t: Why You Shouldn't Try To Convince Difficult Students To Behave udents-to-behave/
q: But in every case, the teacher is trying to convince the student to behave.
Because, when you try to convince students to behave, you’re showing how much it means to you.
You weaken your influence. You’re cede the upper hand in the relationship and give your most challenging students the power to make or break your day.
When there is a crack in the foundation of leadership, however small, your students will fill it—or wrest control of the classroom right out of your hands.
Deliver your news, then turn on your heal and walk away as if nothing happened. Never let them see you sweat.
Your refusal to pull them aside to woo, plead, coax, cajole, or manipulate communicates loud and clear that you believe in them.
Be the leader they need, not the weak-kneed groveler they don’t.

t: How To Put An End To Roughhousing
q: It isn’t uncommon to have otherwise solid classroom management and still struggle to get students to stop wrestling, play-fighting, and the like.
Many students assume that 'keep your hands and feet to yourself' refers only to malicious intent, even if you say otherwise.
Modeling the exact roughhousing behavior you're witnessing, or have witnessed in the past, makes it real and clarifies the definition.
When you model the exact behavior your students are engaging in, and how you’ll enforce it, you’ll see far less of that behavior.
By modeling in the place or places where it occurs, it reframes the act of roughhousing from harmless fun to a stigma they don’t want to be part of.
But the trick is to bring the behavior into sharper focus. It’s to label roughhousing as silly, absurd, and unacceptable within a place of learning—not through your words, but through your actions.
Your students, in turn, will finally make the connection. And refrain from the behavior.

t: How To Get Your Class Back On Track Fast
q: When I returned, it was as if my new class had never met me.
There had been little direction and absolutely no accountability. Now it appeared that the students were in charge.
In the days before coming down with the flu, I laid out exactly what was expected of them, academically and behaviorally.
At the beginning of every season, he would teach his players how to put on their socks. The idea was that if they could do this one thing well, they could do all things well.
I sent them back to their seats (to groans). And I taught them a lesson on how we, the class, enter the room and listen during attendance.

The most gratifying thing about the experience, however, and the most striking change, was their happiness and sense of calm well-being in knowing exactly where they stood and what they needed to do to succeed.
It’s clear and comforting. It’s highly and intrinsically motivational. It’s how education should be.
x: Linsin recounts a personal experience of returning to a new high school class after missing over a week to the flu, only to find their behavior had unraveled under a substitute who never held them accountable.

t: How To Handle Students Who Give You Attitude https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2017/03/04/how-to-handle-students-who-give-you-attitude/
q: They're responses to teacher requests or reminders (i.e. 'Please put your backpack away.') that aren't quite disrespectful. But darn close.
For one, I don’t believe it rises to the level of disrespect. Although it often feels like it, it isn’t directed at you.
Enforcing a consequence, then, often makes things worse, deepening the student’s frustration and discontent.
The way it works is when a student rolls their eyes or gives attitude about something you've said, you're going to smile at them.
It communicates that you don’t give directions because you like bossing people around—which, based on their experience in the past, is how many students view teachers.
The only danger is to be sure you’re clear on the difference between a student having a bad moment and blatant disrespect, which must always be followed by a consequence.
In time, you'll eliminate virtually all 'attitude' from your classroom. And replace it with acceptance, eagerness, and smiles.

Minor attitude — eye rolls, sighs, sarcasm — is usually personal frustration, not disrespect directed at the teacher.
Enforcing a consequence for simple attitude tends to deepen a student's frustration rather than resolve it.
